content: Cannabis use is widespread globally, but there are currently no approved pharmacological treatments for cannabis use disorders. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of various pharmacotherapies compared to placebo, other medications, or no pharmacotherapy (supportive care) in reducing cannabis withdrawal symptoms and promoting cessation or reduction of cannabis use. The review included 21 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a total of 1,755 participants. Most participants were adults (mean age 22 to 41 years), and 75% were male. Three studies focused on younger individuals (mean age 20 years). The studies were generally at low risk of bias, except for one study with selection bias and three studies with attrition bias. All studies compared active medications to placebo, but the diversity of medications and outcomes limited the scope of analysis. Δ9‐tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) preparations did not significantly increase the likelihood of abstinence at the end of treatment compared to placebo (risk ratio [RR] 0.98, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.64 to 1.52; moderate-quality evidence). Similarly, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), mixed-action antidepressants, anticonvulsants, mood stabilizers, buspirone, and N-acetylcysteine showed no significant difference in abstinence rates compared to placebo (lowto very low-quality evidence). There was qualitative evidence suggesting that THC preparations reduced the intensity of withdrawal symptoms compared to placebo. However, for other pharmacotherapies, either this outcome was not examined, or no significant differences were observed. Adverse effects were not more likely with THC preparations (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.17; moderate-quality evidence) or N-acetylcysteine (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.23; moderate-quality evidence) compared to placebo. Similarly, SSRIs, mixed-action antidepressants, buspirone, and N-acetylcysteine did not show an increased likelihood of adverse effects compared to placebo (lowto very low-quality evidence). The likelihood of withdrawal from treatment due to adverse effects was not significantly different for THC preparations, SSRIs, mixed-action antidepressants, anticonvulsants, mood stabilizers, buspirone, or N-acetylcysteine compared to placebo (lowto very low-quality evidence). Treatment completion rates were also similar for THC preparations, SSRIs, mixed-action antidepressants, and buspirone compared to placebo (lowto very low-quality evidence). For N-acetylcysteine, treatment completion rates were slightly higher but not statistically significant (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.21; moderate-quality evidence). However, anticonvulsants and mood stabilizers appeared to reduce the likelihood of treatment completion (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.92; low-quality evidence). There was insufficient evidence to evaluate the effectiveness of gabapentin (an anticonvulsant), oxytocin (a neuropeptide), and atomoxetine. In conclusion, the evidence for all pharmacotherapies investigated remains incomplete, with many outcomes supported by lowor very low-quality evidence. SSRIs, mixed-action antidepressants, bupropion, buspirone, and atomoxetine are likely of limited value in treating cannabis dependence. THC preparations, while still experimental, may have some positive effects on withdrawal symptoms and cravings. The evidence for gabapentin, oxytocin, and N-acetylcysteine is weak, but these medications warrant further investigation.
